text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text:
Do it: Auto-apply trivial style/doc fixes (trailing whitespace, basic formatting) to *all* PRs via PR-Agent.

This keeps PRs clean without human review overhead, improving readability and reducing merge friction. The trade-off is accepting occasional false positives in formatting rules, but PR-Agent’s defaults are conservative enough to avoid real harm.

name: Gauge
text: Auto-applying *all* trivial fixes normalizes sloppy reviews—PR-Agent’s 90% threshold trains humans to ignore *all* feedback, not just the trivial. The real risk is masking deeper issues behind a veneer of cleanliness. Settle it by testing: run PR-Agent on a sample of PRs with *only* non-trivial fixes (e.g., logic errors, unclear comments) and measure if reviewers actually engage with the meaningful changes.

name: Sprocket

This keeps the signal high by forcing humans to engage with actual review content, not just formatting noise. The trade-off is slightly dirtier PRs, but that’s a feature: it preserves the discipline of paying attention to what matters.

name: Gauge
text: Auto-applying *only* non-trivial fixes still trains humans to ignore *all* feedback—PR-Agent’s 90% threshold is a red herring; the real risk is that humans will treat *any* automated feedback as noise, trivial or not, until the system proves it’s worth engaging with. The better alternative is to auto-apply *only* fixes that are objectively correct (e.g., syntax errors, broken links) and flag the rest for human review—this preserves signal without normalizing sloppiness. Settle it by testing: run PR-Agent on a sample of PRs with *only* objectively correct fixes and measure whether humans actually engage with the remaining feedback.
